caption:
Is the Shroud of Turin real?

Radiocarbon dating says no. In 1988 three independent laboratories — Oxford, Arizona and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology — tested a swatch from a corner of the cloth and concluded with 95% confidence that the linen dates from AD 1260–1390. That range matches the first appearance of the shroud in church history: it was exhibited around 1355 in the village church of Lirey, in north-central France.

It was denounced almost immediately. In 1389 the Bishop of Troyes, Pierre d'Arcis, wrote to Antipope Clement VII saying the cloth had been "artificially painted in an ingenious way", and that a previous bishop had identified the artist. Clement allowed exhibitions to continue on one condition: the canons had to say aloud that it was a painting, not the true shroud.

Then in May 1898 the photographer Secondo Pia was permitted to photograph the cloth. On the glass negative the faint sepia stain resolved into a face — clearer in reverse than in life. The Vatican newspaper reported it without comment, then said nothing for nearly half a century. Giuseppe Enrie repeated the result in 1931.

Walter McCrone, examining 1978 tape samples, found red ochre in gelatin and vermilion where the bloodstains are. Other researchers rejected his conclusion.

What is still open: no experiment has reproduced every property of the image at once. The Catholic Church neither endorses nor rejects it.

Images: Secondo Pia's 1898 print; Giuseppe Enrie's 1931 negative; a 1608 copper engraving of an ostension; a fresco at Bessan painted 1503–1522; and a full-length photograph of the cloth. All public domain or CC0.

cards.headline: Enrie repeated it in <y>1931</y> and got the same face
cards.note: Giuseppe Enrie photographed the cloth on 24 May 1931. His negative matched Pia's result.
